utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning, interpreters and technicians. Are you ready? Thank you. Before beginning with this matter before us, please remind us about the matter we have before us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case IT-95-14/1-T, the Prosecutor against Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I see now, Mr. Prosecutor, you have Mr. Niemann, I see, in the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honour pleases, my name is Niemann. I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Meddegoda and Ms. Sutherland for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And for the defence, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Goran Mikulicic, and together with my counsel, co-counsel, Mr. Joka, we act on behalf of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Before beginning, we were informed that it would be appropriate for the Defence and for the Prosecution that we change the calendar to some degree, and so the last week of June, we're not going to be sitting, and we could perhaps transfer that week to the month of August. We were going to end with this case in June or perhaps in July, but if this case goes quite quickly, it must also be fair. And so what we are going to do is try to make this change; you will see what possibilities you might have to drop the last week in June and to move that week to the 3rd of August. After that, we will see what possibilities exist because we must also look at the calendar with the other judges, so we cannot make that decision now here; but as far as these judges are concerned, that is convenient. With that said, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, yesterday Mr. Mikulicic raised the question of whether or not he could have a break in the weeks because of the difficulties he has arranging witnesses. My position on it was that I had certainly no objection to that course, but I said to him that if he was to obtain another date, could he obtain in the second week of August, not the first week of August, because I would be away throughout August -- throughout July and the first week of August, and I only have my colleague, Mr. Meddegoda, now on this case, and because he would be alone on the matter, I had requested that that be the case. If nothing else can be arranged, well, I'm sure Mr. Meddegoda is very capable and able to do in my absence, but I would rather be here, if that was possible. Of course, the dates in June are suitable and acceptable to me because I am here, but it is just in July and the first week of August. So if it is possible, if we could make it that second week in August. I don't know how the progress of matters will go, whether all the time will be consumed with witnesses. I don't know what the position is going to be. I don't expect that, from the Prosecution's point of view, there's going to be much evidence that we will be seeking to call in rebuttal; but, of course, I can't make a judgement about that at the moment because I haven't heard the defence case. But it is possible there will be some rebuttal evidence depending on what emerges as a consequence of the defence case. So it could well take us into August, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, do you have anything you would like to comment on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as my distinguished colleague, Mr. Niemann, has said, yesterday, in respect of the circumstances that were presented, I tried to agree about that with The Prosecution's Office. First of all, as far as the Defence is concerned, it agrees fully with the OTP's proposal that the week in June be transferred to the second week in August as will be convenient for Mr. Niemann because, in the long run, I believe that we will be best proceeding with our cause if we have a consensus between the OTP and the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes. We will take note then of your proposals, but I must tell you in advance that there might be some difficulties for the second week because some of the judges have already planned some travel for that week. So there may be some difficulties in that area, but we will inform you thereof. With that said, let us now begin. Mr. Niemann, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honour pleases, might the witness, Professor Bianchini, be brought to the court? He's in the Prosecution room. The witness room is not available, not open. Your Honours, I have taken the liberty of asking the Registrar to kindly place on the table the exhibits that we tendered yesterday so that they can be at the disposal of Professor Bianchini, so they are there now, and I have asked Professor Bianchini to use the facilities of the overhead projector when referring to exhibits so that it can be easier for all of us to follow. (WITNESS, STEFANO BIANCHINI, continued).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The last time, I believe it was the 26th of February, something like that, you made a solemn declaration to speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. This same solemn declaration is in force. Thank you for coming and thank you also for answering to the questions which will be put to you by Mr. Niemann. Thank you. Examined by MR. NIEMANN.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, on the last occasion, we had reached the point in our discussion where you had told us about a plebiscite that was held in Slovenia on the 23rd of December of 1990. Did there follow in Croatia similarly a plebiscite on May the 19th of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not exactly similar. It should be correct to speak about referendum more than the plebiscite, because the concept of a plebiscite was not included in the Constitution. They hold -- the Government, the Government of Croatia, held the referendum in May 1990. This referendum was based on two questions instead of one, as was the case in Slovenia. The two questions were related to the two proposals submitted in the second half of -- in the previous, 1989, on the confederative and federative perspective of the country. So the Croat people were asked to opt for the confederative proposal submitted by Croat and Slovene leaderships, and the federative proposal prepared by Mr. Jovic. The outcome of the referendum was that less than 83 percent of the eligible voters voted, and of these, 83 percent, 94 percent voted for the perspective of a confederation while only 5 percent and a bit voted for the federative proposal of Mr. Jovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Croatia and Slovenia then subsequently issue Declarations of Independence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did, in June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did they do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In June, 25th June, 1991. The position of the two republics was different. Slovenia made the decision -- the Parliament of Slovenia -- the Parliament made a decision on the same date. Then Croatia, considering that they had -- according to their position -- wanted to implement the decision of the referendum. The referendum, as you remember, invited the population to vote for an independent sovereign state within six months. So at the end of the six months, they wanted to vote on this independence, because any agreement was joined in order to create a confederative Yugoslavia. They voted immediately on a new constitution; they were prepared, from the military and the administrative point of view, to implement the decision immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they," you're referring to Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For Slovenia. For Croatia, it was different. It was different in the sense that Tudjman wanted to maintain a strong lead over the decision, the decision-making with Slovenia. Slovenia decided to declare independence. Tudjman wanted to declare independence on the same day while he was aware that Croatia was not able to implement immediately the decision because it didn't have the military and administrative organisation already prepared for independence. So, for instance, a lot of policy makers in Croatia spoke about that day as the beginning of the process of the session instead of the concluding act of such a decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what ensued as a result of the issuing of these declarations of independence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Slovenia, the result was that the Government immediately order the Slovenian army, supported by the Territorial Defence, to take control of the air space, of the customs, and the borders. And the army did this because it was ready to do this. The reaction of the federal government was very strong because they declared immediately the act, both the act of Slovene aggression, particularly the act of Slovenia, as an illegal act, because it was not agreed upon with the government, and at the same time, because they emphasised the fact -- the decision of Slovenia to take control of the borders was affecting the interests of the other five republics, because through the borders with Italy and Austria, hard currency enters Yugoslavia. This was the reason why the federal government immediately reacted, and then ordered the JNA, particularly the JNA in Slovenia, to take control again of the borders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the JNA. Can you, moving back, tell us what the structure of the armed forces of Yugoslavia was prior to 1990 and then we'll move forward into its role in these events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The structure of the armed forces in Yugoslavia was very specific indeed. You know, it was based on two elements: The first, the JNA, which is the armed forces, and the second was the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to say for the benefit of the people taking down the transcript, by the "JNA," you're referring to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: JNA, is the Yugoslav army, the Yugoslav army, and this was a regular army, and the Territorial Defence. This system was adopted by Tito, by a law approved in February 1969, as a consequence of the Soviet and the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia, when the spring -- the Prague spring was over. They feared that Yugoslavia was -- could be -- would be threatened by the Soviet Union. Nikola Lubicic, he was head of the military -- of the defence at the time, was encouraged to re-think, with the support of Tito, the system of defence of the country, in order to make Yugoslavia, because they didn't have the nuclear [sic], a country where it was impossible to have, for a long time, an army, an occupation army within. And so they re-thought the experience of the partisan period, and they set up the Territorial Defence as a structure able to defend the territory when -- in the event of an attack on the country -- with the typical system of the partisan war. In this sense, for instance, the JNA, the high command of JNA, was the president of the presidency of Yugoslavia. This meant Tito, when Tito was living. And then the president of the presidency, according to article 32A second paragraph of the Constitution 1974. And the Territorial Defence was -- the JNA was -- the JNA was equipped, trained, organised, armed by the federal government, and the Territorial Defence was equipped, trained, and organised by the republics and autonomous regions. So this made possible that in some of the constitutions, the republics’ constitutions, that the presidency of the republic had the power to establish plan for defending the republics. This was the case in Croatia, in the article 3A3 of the Croatian Constitution of 1974, the Socialist Republic of Croatia, it was clearly stated. While this was not the case for Bosnia. It was only -- it was included in the Constitution only in 1989 after -- when an amendment, the 51 amendment was -- changed the article 349 of the Bosnian Constitution, the Socialist Republic of Bosnian Constitution. So this was the structure of the defence, and, if you want, I can show you the ethnic composition of the army with --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I think that you might describe to us the basis of this ethnic key, if you would, and how it operated with respect to the army and perhaps by reference to exhibit 105, which I think is there beside you. And you can put it on the overhead projector. Yes, we have it now. It will be on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is just a table showing the ethnic composition of the JNA in military, professional military and recruits. The source -- this is a table that I prepared on the basis of the figures available in an article written by Anton Bebler. Anton Bebler is the son of the famous diplomat, Yugoslav diplomat, and he is a scholar -- diplomat himself of Slovenian independence, Slovenia in Geneva, and he is particularly known as an expert on military issues. So Anton Bubler prepared this table and, as you can see, you have here three lines: one gives you a picture of the percentage of the population according to the 1981 Yugoslav census. This is a picture, of course, related to the last period of socialist Yugoslavia. So you have here the percentage of the population of each ethnic group of nationalities of Yugoslavia; and then, in the second line, you have the percentage of the professional military in the army. As you can see, for instance, the Serbs were the 36.3 percent in the census 1989 of the whole population of Yugoslavia, but they had a percentage of 60 percent in the professional military; while, as you can see in the third line, you have the percentage of the recruits. This is the recruits, the normal recruits, for the period that they have joined the army, and you can see that the percentage decrease to the 31 percent more or less respecting the percentage of the population, Serb population. You see, for instance, the Croats were 19.8 percent of the population. They had 12.6 percent of the population of military and 18.55 percent of the recruits. If you see the Slovenes, the 7.8 percent of the population, only 2.8 percent in the professional military, and the 7 percent of the recruits. Interesting enough is the figure of Albanians, for instance. 7.7 percent of the population, 0.6 of the military, professional military, and 9 percent of the recruits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what was the consequence, if any, of this disproportionality of representation in the professional ranks of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is very important to take into account, that generally, generally, before the great wave of nationalism was growing in Yugoslavia, that is, until 1986-1987, the main reason why the Serbs joined -- Serbs and Montenegrins -- this is also an interesting data -- the Montenegrins were only 2.5 percent of the population but they had the 6.2 percent of the professional military. So if you can consider this, you see that Serbs and Montenegrins were over-represented in the JNA and the others were underrepresented in the professional military, and the reason was generally because Serbs and Montenegrins shared a tradition in the army, and the second reason was because the army granted a career, a good wage, and prerogatives in areas, particularly for areas -- attractive for areas and developed as it was one part of Serbia, not completely Serbia, but one part of Serbia and Montenegro. In a sense, this kind of approach was confirmed by the Croats in the sense that the Croats particularly -- overwhelmingly joined the navy thanks because of-- its the stronger nation. So this was the reason why you have this kind of picture when you are still this period. The number of the army, of the JNA, decreased from the beginning of the '80s today and of the case from 220,000 people to 180,000, and the air forces were around 33,000 people. Then we have no figures, exact figures, we didn't have the exact figure about the navy, while the navy was a small part of the JNA, a small one. About the Territorial Defence, we have different figures. According to Slovene sources, they were around 500,000 people involved in whole Yugoslavia, and according Bosnian sources, they were around 700,000. So this was generally the picture of the army structure of JNA until the beginning of the '90s. What is interesting enough, it seems to me, is to compare this general structure with the high commands of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could tell us about that and, at the same time, place on the screen exhibit 106? Would you keep the exhibits in order, Professor, so we don't ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes. I prepared this also. I prepared this picture just to show you the structure of the commands of the JNA at the time when Ante Markovic was the Premier, so in second half 1989 and in 1990. As you can see, the ethnic composition of the communists is still very Yugoslav. The federal Minister of Defence was General Kadijevic. Kadijevic, at the time, declared himself as a Yugoslav, which was a very disputed declaration because, in a sense, those who declared themselves Yugoslavs, as you remember, were put at the end of the list of ethnic groups. But just to make it clear, the origin of Kadijevic, his father was Serb, his mother and wife were Croats. He came from, the soldiers were from the area of Krajina, Croatian Krajina. The vice-minister was the Admiral Stane Brovet, a Slovene. The head of the general command of the General Staff, as you can see, General Stevo Mirkovic, who was a Serb, and when he retired -- he retired in the period of the government of Ante Markovic, -- so he was replaced by Blagoje Adzic, again a Serb. The president of the communist organisation of the army, this is a very important structure, was Admiral Petar Simic, a Croat from Bihac. He is from Bosnia-Herzegovina. The communist organisation of the army was very important. They had 100,000 members in that period, so this was more or less, as I mentioned, half or more than half of the people involved in the army. I mentioned between 220,000, 180,000 people. So this was a powerful organisation, with hardly any control by the civilian organisation of the League of the Communists on. So they acted as a closed organisation within the league of Communists. The head of the Air Forces was Anton Tus, a Croat. The heads of the four military areas were from the Skopje area, Zivota Avramovic, a Serb. From Zagreb, the Zagreb area, Martin Spegelj, a Croat. When he retired in the period of the Markovic government, he was replaced by Konrad Kolisek, a Slovene. In the Split area, the head was Admiral Bozo Grubisic, a Croat, and in Belgrade area, Anton Lukezic, a Croat, and when he retired, he was replaced by Alexandar Spirkovski, a Macedonian. As you can see, this picture offers you a different image than that presented before. As you can imagine, the 60 percent of professional military of Serbs were -- particularly in the middle, the officials in the middle ranks, while the top of the JNA composition was very Yugoslav, according to the principle that started in the period of Tito, the Second World War, until 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did the break-up of the former Yugoslavia, and we've referred to the declarations of independence of Slovenia and Croatia, have any, and if so what, impact upon the JNA? And the forces of these changes that were to take place, did they impact upon the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The impact during the '80s was very significant. The significant impact on the position of not only Slovenia and Croatia but even of Serbia. If I can just mention here one event, a significant event in the context of Slovene area. This happened in the second half of the '80s when the editorial board of Mladina, a very known and popular magazine in Ljublijana and Janez Jansa was one of the members of the editorial board when they published and were charged by the army of spreading military secrets. So this is the reason they were arrested and a trial took place in Ljublijana. The trial was carried out in Serbo-Croat and not in the Slovene language. This was particularly considered a demonstration -- this was considered by the leadership, the Slovenian leadership, by Kucan, particularly, but the whole Slovene leadership, as a demonstration of the wish of the Serb leadership to control Yugoslavia and to have a dominant position, a dominant position in the army and in Yugoslavia. Kucan started his charges in a meeting of the presidency, of the federal presidency, and for the first time, because he never did this before, he spoke in the Slovene language during the presidency and then he reported the same speech in a meeting of Ljublijana in the Slovene language. This was one element that created a great conflict between the Slovene leadership and JNA command. Other elements that created conflicts were the requests coming particularly from the organisations of the youth in Slovenia to have legitimised their conscious objectives -- conscious objections --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Conscientious objections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. Later, the government and the Slovene leadership tried also to diminish the defence budget and the financial support of the Yugoslav Federation towards the army. These elements created tensions between the JNA command and the Slovene leaderships. This was one event. Another event about Croatia, about Croatia, a very significant event took place in January 1991 when the ministry -- at the time, the Ministry of Defence, Martin Spegelj, who had been one of the Generals in the JNA army, you can find his name, he was the command head of the Zagreb area, but once retired, he was called as a minister -- by Tudjman as minister of Defence of Croatia. Martin Spegelj was filmed by the Secret Service speaking with the Croat Minister of Interior about the importation, illegal importation, of a great amount -- a great number of weapons from Hungary. This film was broadcast on television and the army tried to arrest him. He was protected by Tudjman and this situation created such strong tensions between the Croat leadership and the JNA army that a temporary compromise was found at the end of the month when the army remained in its headquarters in Croatia and the Territorial Defence of Croatia was, at least, partially dismantled. But let me say that a very important impact was also the Serb attitude towards the army in that period. My personal belief is that the Serb leadership when Milosevic controlled it completely, that after Stambolic, the President of Serbia, was compelled to resign. After 1987 the first real goal of the Serb leadership was not the control over the whole of Yugoslavia. If you read carefully, the Memorandum of the Serb Academy of Science in -- particularly, the last sentences -- you can see that the last sentences are very clear in this sense because it's claimed that if Serbia, whether Serbia cannot have its own role in Yugoslavia based on its demographic strength, its historical legacy, on its state which was denied by the constitution in 1974, and so on. So it was better for Serbia to have an alternative to Yugoslavia, as well as Croatia and Slovenia had in the past, which means that the real proposal of the memorandum was to take into account the possibility for Serbia to abandon the federation. You know, to change the constitution, the Yugoslav constitution, you need consensus. So the agreement of the leadership of Croatia or Slovenia or Macedonia, it is quite difficult to think that these leaderships, communist or partly communist after the election of 1990, were able to accept to diminish their own rights or the rights of their republics in order to follow the request of the silent/secret memorandum. This is very difficult to realise, but there are other elements, of course, that show that this was particularly the orientation of Milosevic. This had a particular impact in relations between Serbia and the army in the months to come. If we think that Serbia really wanted to abandon the federation, we have other elements that can confirm this orientation. For instance, in January 1991, six months before the war erupted in Yugoslavia, Milan Kucan and Slobodan Milosevic met in Belgrade. It was in the second half of the month. They had delegations, so I received information from one of the witnesses in this delegation, a Slovene. During this meeting, Kucan asked Milosevic to abandon Slovenia without any war and Milosevic agreed to this position under the condition that, in a way, Kucan publicly recognised the right of Serbia to have its own state with only the Serbs included in this state. In fact, if you check the day after this meeting, the newspapers published -- all the newspapers in Yugoslavia published a declaration in which -- in a not completely clear way, but anyway, it appears that Kucan accepted the idea that Serbs had the right to live in the same state. This created great tensions between Croatia and Slovenia. The Slovene leadership was accused by the Croatian public opinion of stabbing Croatia in the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why? Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why? Because, as you can imagine, if Slovenia -- Slovenia was, as you remember in the table presented at the beginning last time, Slovenia was more or less -- 90 percent of the people living in Slovenia were Slovenes. So, Slovenia was more or less a mono-ethnic republic, the only mono-ethnic republic in the former Yugoslavia, while in Croatia, 11 percent of the population was made up of Serbs in Krajina, in the cities, in Dalmatia, in Slavonia. If you recognise the right of Slovenia to leave Yugoslavia peacefully, and at the same time you recognise the right of the Serbs to live all together in the same state, all you move is all the population from Croatia and from Bosnia to Serbia proper or you have to take into account the issue of borders as open -- within the other parts of -- so this was the reason of the election of Croatia. Our state is now under threat from Belgrade, from the republic’s leadership in Belgrade, to lose one part of his territory, of this republic’s territory, because it was occupied predominantly in some parts by Serbs. This was the case of the area of Krajina. This was the reason why Croatia was afraid for this. Then, consider that it was very, very peculiar how the war was conducted in Slovenia. The war was very short and in this case, immediately after four or five days of war, the mothers of the Serb recruits went to Slovenia to pick up their children and came back home. This happened only in Slovenia. This didn't happen in Croatia. It didn't happen in Bosnia. This is important because I think that Milosevic didn't allow this to be repeated, though it was allowed once, because it was an agreement with Kucan to leave Slovenia peacefully and the decision was made about other subjects, the government, the army, which had no similar goals at the beginning as Milosevic. Third, let me say again, in other elements, in July 1991, when the presidency met for the first time after several months complete with the Slovenia representative, Drnovsek, the current president of the Slovenian government, they voted on role of the JNA in Slovenia. Jovic, the Serb, and Drnovsek agreed immediately about this while a Croat representative, Mesic, voted against and this request, the decision to withdraw the army from Slovenia, was not requested by the international community. This was a decision made in the presidency with the agreement of the members of the presidency but with the negative vote of the Croat representative. The outcome was clear because upon withdrawal of the army from Slovenia, the army went to Croatia and created the condition for the war in Croatia, while Croatia was not prepared militarily nor administratively, to implement the declaration of independence of June. They wanted to join Slovenia only because of the period at the time. These were the elements that make it clear, from my point of view, that the Milosevic’s real goal was the cessation of Serbia from Yugoslavia. This is not something crazy or something that appeared strange. Yeltsin, at the end of the 80's also threatened Gorbachev to withdraw Russia from the Soviet Union. This was one interesting aspect of this cessation -- this was the cessation of the main republic and the main demographic republic from the Federation, instead of the others. This had also impact on the military because the military, you know, they had a different -- just at the beginning, particularly the commanders, not the middle ranks, but the commanders had a different position. They were communists. All these people you have here, they were communists. They were members of the communist organisation in the army. They believed in Yugoslav communism and they wanted to preserve communism. Also, you know, they had privileges, prerogatives, they had played a peculiar role in Yugoslavia for a long period -- during the 40's, the 50's, the 60's, they had a very good image in the country, they were appreciated as the army which had liberated the country. It was the army which protected the country against Stalin. These elements created the positive attitude of the population towards the army. These old commanders were, in this sense, very attached to the idea of Yugoslavia, to the idea of communism, and they wanted to preserve it while communism was collapsing all over Eastern Europe and not only in Yugoslavia. Then they also had, all the military, may I say, an actual bent for Jovic, so they wanted to open -- they wanted to -- and they are afraid about the dismantlement of Yugoslavia, but from the point of view of the communist integration system. So this was their approach at the beginning. The situation changed in the following months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I might ask you to speak a little bit slower, if you would, because it is hard for the interpreter. Why then could Milosevic have an agreement with Kucan when it involved the JNA which wasn't directly under his control? How was it he was able to do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, at the beginning, Milosevic didn't have complete control of the army. He could have control of the army only through changes in the military. Changes started when, for instance, between the end of 1989 and 1990, many Generals retired because they reached retirement age. So the ranks, the middle ranks, had the opportunity to have a career. These ranks were particularly attracted by Milosevic's strong attitudes. Let me say that in 1988 Kadijevic had already submitted a proposal to the federal presidency in order to amend the Yugoslav constitution and to create a strong presidency. They were, at that time, already -- they already feared for the future of the country and they particularly opposed the idea of having a weak federal presidency. The proposal was rejected, but it is interesting anyway this time, because at the beginning this showed their attitude of the army towards hierarchy and order. We can also consider that at the beginning, in 1986 and 1987 when the policy of meeting -- the so-called national political meeting, anti-bureaucratic revolution organised by Milosevic in Kosovo first, and then in Vojvodina, and then in Montenegro created a negative attitude in the army. But the sensitivity towards the criticism coming from Slovenia was much more higher than the criticism towards the attitudes of Milosevic. So when Milosevic because had this strong attitude and the Generals retired, the middle ranks had the opportunity to have a career and they were much more sensitive and reacted much more positively to the attitude of Milosevic than thinking that Milosevic in such a way would preserve Yugoslavia or at least would save the role of the Serbs within Yugoslavia in a very -- protecting their role within Yugoslavia as the Serbs were, according to the propaganda of Serbia, threatened by the other republics -- which was not true -- but this was the general attitude.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Kadijevic fear the existence of the TO during this period and why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kadijevic in January 1990, in an article written by -- not an article, a journal of the army published an article where he wrote about -- he wrote about the risk that the Territorial Defence might be transformed into a Republican army. I mentioned that, on the basis of some constitutions, it was not only in the case of Croatia, but in Bosnia in 1989. The Republic had the right to prepare plans for defence of the Republic and the Republic had the task of training, and arming and equipping the Territorial Defence. So for this reason, Kadijevic feared that the Territorial Defence would become the Republican army and suggested the possibility of dismantling it. This was one reason. The other reason was generally the JNA since 1969 hadn’t accepted very positively the creation of the Territorial Defence, but this is also another aspect of this. Anyway, it was only on May 23rd, 1990, it is when the change of the president of the presidency was over and Drnovsek ended his period, and Borisav Jovic, and this was the time of Borisav Jovic, that he was a man close to Milosevic, a Serb, that it was possible to establish an order from the president of the presidency to move all the weapons from the stores of the Territorial Defence to the stores of the JNA. This was a decision suggested by Kadijevic and approved by Jovic in May 1990. So this was the period. And according to the memoirs published later by Kadijevic, it was more of a general -- this was published in Belgrade, it is written that this attempt at moving the weapons from the stores of the JNA to the -- from the stores of the Territorial Defence to the stores of the JNA was successful everywhere in Yugoslavia, except in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we've spoken of events that occurred in both Slovenia and in Croatia in 1991. Did that also have an impact on the ethnic composition of the JNA during the course of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1991, in the first half of 1991, it's difficult to say because some changes were in the army but not, for instance, in the high command. It was not, for instance, by chance, this is interesting, that when the war occurred in Slovenia, the first people who died in Slovenia from the JNA side were Slovene recruits. So in this sense, the army had still -- at that point, they still had a Yugoslav structure, but immediately after the end -- when the war in Slovenia erupted the recruits were -- flew recruits from Slovenia first, and then the recruits from Croatia, from Bosnia, Macedonia, through the camp, the army, so the army became the normal Serb army while the other changes in the commands had to take -- had to be imposed by Milosevic, particularly during 1992, in order to reorganise the army. So this was again a period where the mentality -- the mentality of the army, while already influenced by the Milosevic approach, thought and wanted to operate in order to save the communist Yugoslavia which was, in fact, over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving on to Bosnia, did there come a time when the Bosnian Serbs proceeded to clear autonomous regions in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. The Serbs -- may I just offer -- show a map?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Tell us the exhibit number that you are looking at. It's on the back. Okay. That's exhibit 107. And the map that you have there, exhibit 107, what's that about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a map -- I can't see on the monitor. It doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You need to press "Computer Monitor." Can you see on your -- the button there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah, sorry. Yes, okay. Thank you. This map has been prepared by me with the help of the office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Try "Computer Monitor."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. This prepared -- was prepared here in -- by the officers of the Tribunal under my direction and was prepared on the basis of the documents I collected from Serb side about the Constitution of the Serb autonomous region, the so-called SAO. This was the political process known as Saoizacija, the transformation of Bosnia in SAO regions. There were six regions. It started in second half of 1991. It started with -- in the area of Banja Luka creating a series of -- community of municipalities it was called, like this, and then later, from September, in the period from September to January -- from September '91 to January 1992, six Serb autonomous regions were created. You see here on different colours these regions. The first one was the area of Herzegovina, this is the blue part, and then was created the area of Banja Luka, the SAO Bosanska Krajina, and then you have the SAO Romanija, on the back of Sarajevo, the SAO Semberjia area in the area of Bijeljina and then SAO Sjeverne Bosnia, and then you see also the area that were not -- this I wanted to include as Bosansko Grahovo, Bosanski Novi, Bosanska Dubica and Bosanska Gradiska. You see in these areas in grey colour, these areas were not included in the official documents I collected, so officially they were not part of these regions, but they were, in fact, under the control of the Serbs. This is very interesting in reality -- actually, the documents were -- of the Serbs were not very precise in explaining the areas they claimed exactly because, for instance, the municipality of Visegrad, here on the eastern side of Bosnia close to the River Drina belonged to two different SAO areas, so it was claimed by one and by the others. So this was a picture -- a picture just to give you an idea of this process of areas which is interesting, more or less, in order to understand the areas claimed by SDS -- SDS was the Serb Democratic Party led by Karadzic and who was in the government in Bosnia at the time, and this showed the area in a sense that the SDS claimed as area under the control -- that must be under the control of the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there reaction in Bosnia to these declarations of autonomous regions that occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, the reaction was generally very negative, very negative because -- and it was considered a decision -- an illegal decision. There were no regions included in the Constitution. The Constitution of Bosnia -- Bosnia was, at that time, a socialist republic, the Constitution was amended but not changed, so the change of the Constitution was, in a way, declared only in 1993 when the war between -- not only between the Serbs and the Muslims, but even between the Muslims and the Croats was on. So this was, in this sense, this was the step for preparing a dismemberment of Bosnia and this was the area that Muslims and Croats considered the claims of Serbs over the part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the Muslim and Croat members of the Bosnian parliament do about this issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In October --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- in October 1991, in the parliament, the Croat and the Muslim representatives of the HDZ, SDA, Croat party, and as they are the party led by Izetbegovic voted a resolution on the sovereignty of Bosnia. The SDS representatives didn't participate in the vote, so the SDS didn't recognise the vote as a legal vote. The Croats and Muslim representatives, HDZ, SDA, voted for a sovereign Bosnia in -- during -- so this was another element of tension between two -- the two groups. While it's important to say that SDS, HDZ and SDA shared power at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the SDS subsequently, in November, then proceed to have a referendum or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in November 9, the SDS, as a reaction to the decision on the vote in the parliament by the Muslim and the SDR, vote claim -- organised a plebiscite, plebiscite for establishing the wish for -- declaring the wish of the Serb people to maintain close ties and to remain in the Yugoslav framework, so close ties with Belgrade confirmed. And, of course, the vote was not -- the vote was overwhelmingly in favour of the Serb SDS position while we have no -- any demonstration proved that the vote was fair and democratic, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this atmosphere of rising tensions in Yugoslavia and in the environment of Eastern Europe generally at this period of time, did the European Foreign Ministers meet in Brussels in December for the purposes of setting guidelines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You know, the situation, the general situation in autumn 1991 was very peculiar, a lot of things were changing. In the context of Yugoslavia, the war was characterised by the bombardments of Dubrovnik, of Vukovar, and the battle in Osijek; this is Slovenia and Dalmatia. In this context, we had also the coup in the Soviet Union and the beginning of the process of dismemberment of the Soviet Union. So many states claimed in this context recognition of their independence from the former federal frameworks. On the other side, you had -- at the beginning of -- this is interesting enough -- at the beginning of December, 10th, 11th, a meeting of the representatives of the European Union in Maastricht when they made the decision to increase integration processes, and they made the decision -- the decision when -- when start to do with the single currency in 1998. So in this context of changes, of contradictory changes in the European framework, the Ministers of Foreign Affairs of the European Union met in the midst of December, 16th of December, and they made a decision to write down guidelines of -- for recognition of new state of Eastern Union -- of Eastern Europe and Soviet Union, so this was a general framework. Interestingly enough, in this framework, it was established that the request to be recognised by the new state had to be followed by the recognition that borders were -- about the inviability [sic] of the borders, which meant that, in fact, the administrative borders of the republic within the federal frameworks had to be accepted as international borders, and then, of course, this recognition about the inviability of borders had to be followed by the recognition of democracy, of human rights, of all these crucial elements that characterise the transition towards democratic states. On the basis of this, it was also -- prepared a specific document for the Yugoslav context, and the Yugoslav republics claiming recognition were invited to submit an application form, may I say, application form to the European Union, deadline was December the 3rd, explaining the reason why they wanted to be recognised as independent states with, interesting enough, guarantees that they accept, not change -- they accepted the borders not to be changed with violence, and so only through negotiations in the case, and according to the international standards of respecting human rights, democracy, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These applications, when submitted, had to be scrutinised and analysed by anyone in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When these applications, submitted by the republics of Yugoslavia, when they were submitted, were they then to be scrutinised by a person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- no, no. Yes, sir, they appointed a commission of five lawyers, constitutional lawyers. This was an international European commission led by a lawyer Badinter, a French lawyer, who had the task to refer to the commission by January 10th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Badinter then subsequently receive the applications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Badinter received four applications; that is, the applications of Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Macedonia. They didn't receive any application from Serbia or Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did Badinter commence his work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Badinter Commission ended its work in January. You know, this was a decision made because there were many tensions within the European Commission, particularly between the French position and the German position. France wanted to have, in a way, a common decision about recognition. Germany wanted and applied pressure to have a unilateral recognition of Slovenia and Croatia. So Badinter received the application and the Commission met, and then they suggested to the Commission that, on the basis of the documents presented and the guarantee requested, they suggested recognising the independence of Slovenia and Macedonia. This was the proposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the Commission, headed by Badinter, do this by a way of a number of opinions that were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They received from Badinter a series of opinions. Each opinion was related to a country, so you had the opinion number 2 about Croatia, another opinion about -- the number 4 was about Bosnia, the number 6 on Slovenia. So they had several opinions, and from each opinion, the evolution of the situation followed the countries. So they suggested the independence only for -- the recognition of independence only for Slovenia and Macedonia while the decision of the Commission was different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what was the position with respect to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About the position of Bosnia, the Commission stated that a clear option for an independent sovereign state in Bosnia at the moment didn't exist. They noticed that, in the meantime, when the Badinter Commission was looking at the forms, the assembly of the Serbs, so-called assembly of the Serbs. It was, in fact, an assembly adopted by the SDS party outside the Bosnian parliament, started in the end of December and at the beginning, the 9th of January; that is, one day before the Badinter Commission -- had to defer to the Commission, they informed that they created -- they proclaimed the Republic of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So this was the first aspect. The second aspect was that in the amendments in the Constitution of Bosnia was stated that people wield the power through the mediation of an assembly or a referendum. So for this reason, they proposed -- submitted a proposal that the position was not clear because the Serb part had a different opinion that -- the part expressed by the other ethnic groups of Bosnia. And in this sense, Badinter Commission suggested holding a referendum in Bosnia in order to know the exact position -- exact opinion of the population of Bosnia on the basis of the Constitution, Bosnian Constitution, on the issue of an independent sovereign state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did Badinter suggest this, that a referendum be held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Referendum was suggested after the 10th of January when the Commission had to make the decision about the recognition, when the so-called "Avis" -- the original were written in French -- they were made public and were discussed by the Commission. So it was embodied in the addendum numero 4, avis number 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the question, can you remember, that was to be asked of the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decision was made in January, in the end of January, by the parliament, Bosnian parliament, to order referendum, and decision was made with the agreement of the HDZ, SDA, and (indiscernible) position parties in the parliament, while the SDS representatives didn't take part to the decision, they were not in the parliament when the decision was made. So this was the position of those who claimed the referendum, and the -- may I refer to my notes just to read the question, the question, the exact term of the question submitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the witness have permission to refer to his notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. They submitted was this one: "Are you in favour of an independent and sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina as a State" -- this is very important -- "of equal citizens?" This is the first sentence, "equal citizens." "People of Bosnia-Herzegovina," second sentence, then "(Muslims, Serbs, and Croats) and members of other peoples living in it?" This was the sentence approved by the parliament and submitted to the referendum in 1992, March 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the outcome of the referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We have --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you might --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This, Your Honours, for the record, is exhibit 108.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The outcomes -- because the outcome of the referendum was very interesting. As you can see, the voters were only the 65.31 percent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's because the Serbs didn't participate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbs -- we can presume that overwhelmingly the Serbs didn't vote, but because the non-voters were 35.69 percent, and according to the census, the Serbs were 34 -- 31 percent or less, this means to one part of others, we don't know, maybe Yugoslavs, maybe Jews, maybe others. We don't know. We can't be sure. Then we can be totally sure that overwhelmingly the Serbs didn't vote and the others voted. This is just to give you a picture. And this is interesting. 99.44 percent of those who voted, voted in favour of the question for a sovereign Bosnia of citizens and peoples. This means -- and this is the percentage I wanted to include in the end of this table -- that if you consider the impact of this 99.44 percent of "Yes" on the framework of all the eligible voters of Bosnia, that is including the non-voters, you have a percentage of "Yes" for the state -- for independent state of 63.95 percent of population of Bosnia who accepted the idea of independence. So this means that all but the 35 people didn't vote. If we state that this was a negative vote, we have, in any case, a large majority of people claiming independent sovereignty of Bosnia in 1992. This was between February and March 29 -- 3rd of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this referendum, and particularly after the results of this referendum became known, what was the Serb response, the Bosnian-Serb response?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, immediately after -- when the assembly, the assembly of Bosnia made a decision to order referendum, SDS leadership made clear that because the decision was made without their representative, SDS representative in the Serb parliament, the referendum had to be considered an instrument that obliged only Croatian and Muslim population but not the Serbs. The Serbs considered this as a referendum not in -- not involving Serb population, so as a decision made that it was not of -- within the interests and within the orientation of the Serb population. Then the -- on the basis of this decision, the municipalities of Bosnia were -- mayors or the Serbs were in general a majority, they boycotted the referendum; in fact, they didn't support -- they didn't accomplish their duties in order to make the vote possible. So the Republican Electoral Commission had to set up and appoint new members of the local electoral commission in order to create election stations, voting stations, all over the country, and, in fact, they succeed in it except for Drvar and Bosansko Grahovo, they're the only two municipalities where the voting stations were not created. This was the reaction before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what happened after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately after, on -- on March, two, three days after the referendum, barricades were set up in Sarajevo, and the tension was very high in the country. Then the tension diminished and an attempt of mediation started again with the European Union before the parliament of Bosnia proclaimed independence of Bosnia. Bosnia was recognised on April 6th by the European Commission and followed, the day after, by the recognition of the United States which recognised not only Bosnia but even Croatia and Slovenia. The United States recognised only the day after the recognition of Bosnia by the European Union, even Slovenia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as a consequence of all of these events, did military hostilities then ensue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You know, we don’t have a clear -- an exact date of the beginning of the war. We can consider that the official date is April 6th when snipers, Serb snipers, shot at a peaceful demonstration for peace in Sarajevo from the rooms of the Holiday Inn Hotel in Sarajevo in 1992, but tensions already arose before. It's true that these tensions were sporadic events. They didn't create a real process. But if you look back chronologically, this is interesting to see, this evolution of events. As, for instance, in September 1991, a mobilisation of the JNA was proclaimed in Bosanska Krajina which is an area inhabited predominantly by Serbs. In October, irregulars, Serb irregulars backed by JNA, destroyed -- burned and destroyed the village of Ravno close to Trebinje. Ravno was a village inhabited by Croats and other villages around Ravno. And then in -- this was in October. In November, the bridges on the Sava River were -- if you want, I can show you on the map. Again, we can show the same map just to show what is Ravno. You see Bosnia in the blue, blue area, this area, this is the area of Trebinje, and Ravno is more or less in this area. So it started -- the mobilisation, the Bosanska Krajina was here, the area of Banja Luka, this was the area. And then you had this attack against Ravno by irregular Serbs in October. In November, the bridges of the Sava River here were mined. Between February and March of 1992, there were several explosions. Tensions occurred in Slavonski Brod on the north of Bosnia, then in Banja Luka, then in Mostar, and then I think that probably the most critical situation was that in Bijeljina at the beginning of April, the 3rd of April, 1992. It is here in the corner, in the north-east corner of Bosnia. When irregulars, Serb irregulars, the so-called Tigrovi, the Tigers, organised by Arkan, from other sources, particularly HVO sources spoke about also the participation of Cetnici, which were the members of the group led by Seselj, the current Vice Premier of the Serb government. Anyway, both -- the Tigrovi came from Banja Luka after having participated in the attack against Vukovar, and they arrived in Bijeljina and they attacked the city and they killed a hundred of the Muslim population, forcing the other part of the population to abandon the city. So this was the most serious event that happened before the so-called "official" starting of the war April 6th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these irregular forces, headed by Arkan and Seselj, in any way supported by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally, the Arkan, the Tigrovi, as well as the Cetnici, were supported by JNA, were backed by JNA, sometimes backed and supported directly from Serbia or Montenegro. The, for instance, events in Ravno were particularly backed by people coming from Montenegro. This is understandable -- if you look on the map, this is the area where Bosnia has its border with Montenegro. In addition, the army, the JNA army, supplied Tigrovi, Cetnici, and other irregular groups, the Beli Orlovi, the White Eagles of Ante Markovic, from a little extremist party, the Serb Renewal Parties, and they received weapons, ammunitions. They were supported particularly -- we had also document, a very interesting document, by -- signed by General Blagoje Adzic, who was the -- in fact, he was the new Minister of Defence of Yugoslavia at the time, where he ordered the JNA to establish command over all these irregular Serb groups. So this was the reason why we can -- yes, we -- the JNA supported and helped these irregular units, irregular units in this period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. It is now eleven o'clock, or a quarter to eleven o'clock, and we have a lot of work ahead of us. We know that Mr. Bianchini is speaking with a great deal of enthusiasm about this matter, but we also know that he can become tired, and I see that Mr. Aleksovski is also becoming fatigued. Perhaps it would be wise to take a recess for one hour because we're going to see the inauguration ceremony for the second courtroom. So around a quarter to noon, perhaps, we will resume? Are you in agreement with this? Very well. We stand in recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: --- Reconvened at 12.03 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Well, the official inauguration of the second courtroom took place. However, tomorrow, you will have the opportunity to inaugurate the work in the second courtroom, I can tell you now that it is a very nice courtroom, very beautiful courtroom, and it shows that justice can indeed be carried out, particularly with very good communication because one is very close to the other in that courtroom, and so at 9.00 tomorrow we will be working in that courtroom, and I think that is definitely an improvement for the Tribunal. Mr. Prosecutor, Mr. Niemann, you have the floor. We are going to continue the hearing with a great deal of attention, the testimony given by the professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, before the adjournment, we had been talking about the referendum that was held in Bosnia-Herzegovina relating to the issue of independence of Bosnia. I ask you what the position of the Bosnian Serbs was to this referendum. What was the position, if any, to the referendum, by the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a very interesting issue because the HRZ, the Bosnian-Croat party, while it voted for the referendum -- for holding the referendum in January and approving at the beginning the question, as I read in the former session, in February 9th, in a meeting in Livno, they proposed to change the question. The question was very interesting. May I refer to the notes and read the second version of the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With Your Honours' permission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second question submitted at that meeting was the following: "Are you in favour of an independent, sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina, community state of titular, sovereign peoples, Croatian, Muslim and Serb, in their own national areas," and in brackets "cantons", which means that -- take into consideration the former question. The other question added the term "citizens" first and then "the peoples," and no connection, no relation between people and territory. While in this question, you don't have any mention of the role of citizenship of the individuals, but only they stressed the collective right of the groups in connection with the question of the territories. They envisaged, in fact, what was one of the possible strategies of the evolution of Bosnia in a kind of union of crusades. This question created a lot of tensions between Croats and Muslims before the vote, so when you take into account the result -- may I just show again here the table with the results of the referendum?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is, sorry. This is exhibit 108. When you see this list of eligible voters of 64.31 percent or, if you want, the 99.44 percent of the "yes" votes are of those who went to vote, you have to take into account that because of the tensions which arose around the question, the two parties, SDA and HDZ, went to the referendum having in mind two different things about the future of Bosnia. They agreed about the independence, but how to organise after this independence, how to establish the contacts and the relations within the ethnic groups, and maybe with the tables, this was a completely different question. This was a vote, but having in mind the two parties had in mind two different perspectives. This is clear because of the tension which arose in February 1992, which is a very interesting month because this was the month when the president of HDZ, Stjepan Kljujic, was forced to resign and Mate Boban became the new president.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then went on before the break to speak of the commencement of hostilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina which ensued after the results of the referendum were known. Can you, in summary, tell us the forces that were arraigned against each other in relation to this conflict and have the composition of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the three armies?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have a new table in this sense, but I would like to stress -- this is the exhibit 109. It's very difficult, however, to have an exact picture of the forces right, so that's why I thought that it was better to offer to you a picture where you can see different evolution from different sources. The sources are German or British or in Croatian from Nedjeljna Dalmacija, which was and which is a very popular journal, newspaper, weekly -- daily, sorry, in Split. Connecting all this data, you can have very different pictures about the forces. As you can see, Bosnian-Muslims were on the basis of -- for instance, they reported 210,000 while there were even 1,000 on the status administered by McNeil-Lehrer or even 164,000 by Jane's Defence Weekly. As you can see also, the number of the Bosnian Serbs changed drastically. If you wanted to see, you can move from 20,000 -- 60,000 people, sorry, the International Institute for Strategic Studies from London and to 102,000, according to the Jane's Defence Weekly. But it seems to be very interesting, the studies of the International Institute for Strategic Studies, because it's very known and famous in Britain and very serious. These dates are from 1993 -- 1994, sorry, and as you can see, for Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Serbs, they are not only the number of the soldiers belonging to each party, but they are the reserve units or the back armies, the armies that backed the organisations, for instance, the Croatian army and the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that served in Montenegro. This was their evolution. What is very interesting, that in their evolution, you have at least 15,000 soldiers of the official Croatian army were fighting in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as 20,000 people of the official army of Serb Montenegro Federation. This is just to give you a picture so that when you have different evolutions of different sources about how the forces arranged and facing each other during the conflict, at least before -- this is the picture before the Oluja offensive. This is before the offences of 1995, the period until 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you spoke of the various factors influencing the outbreak of the conflict. Can you draw those together for us and give us your opinion of what gave rise to the commencement of the armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina in summary form?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, it's a common opinion, largely shared by policy makers, as it's called, public opinion, that the forces who gave rise in the conflict were particularly linked to Serb nationalism. And this is true. However, I would like to stress immediately that it's impossible to consider the Bosnian conflict as a conflict separate of the general framework of the Yugoslav dismemberment. My firm belief is that no war in Bosnia were possible whether Yugoslavia didn't disintegrate. The war in Bosnia has to be considered an episode, a tragic episode, the most tragic episode until now, but always an episode of the Yugoslav disintegration in the Yugoslav war. You can take into consideration the political situation of Bosnia before the war erupted. After the election in 1990, you had three parties who won the elections, SDA led by Izetbegovic, SDS led by Graz and HDZ led by Njivice. Muslim, Serb and Croat parties, they were forced to govern together in Bosnia in November, December 1990 when Ante Markovic was still the premier and a presidency, a Yugoslav presidency, existed with six, plus two members. But they had since then three different perspectives, political options. SDS, the Karadzic party, wanted to close ties with Belgrade and claimed these closed ties, possibly to saving and maintaining the Yugoslav Federation in any case, while the HDZ claimed to have closed ties with Zagreb. Even SDA had no clear option in this sense, in the sense they wanted to establish close connection with another part of Yugoslavia where Slav Muslims were the majority. This was Sandzak. Sandzak is an area in between Montenegro and Serbia, and divided by Montenegro and Serbia, where a majority of Slav Muslims as the Muslims of Bosnia are, are living there. They had this idea and, in fact, in the Sandzak, it existed, a party, with the same name of the Izetbegovic party, the SDA. In this sense, you see, you have the HDZ in Croatia and the HDZ in Bosnia with the same name. The SDA, the Izetbegovic party in Bosnia, and the SDA party in Sandzak between Montenegro and Serbia, and then SDS, the party of Karadzic, which has no connection with the SDS, the senior party in Serbia led by Micunovic and then by other leaderships. He had much more strong ties directly with Milosevic. The three options of the party, it clashes urgently. It was evident that if a coalition were prepared at that time in 1981, only including two of these three parts, immediately would create the condition for the war. But because Yugoslavia existed, the three parties were forced to stay together and, in a way, to manage the situation while, in fact, it was impossible to organise something because one of the parties blocked out the other two, when they had to vote. When Yugoslavia collapsed, the war was important because it was a part of the tensions that arose generally in the Yugoslav framework. The Yugoslav events and the Bosnian events are strictly connected and can't be considered separately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in all this, what role, then, during 1992, in the course of 1992, did the JNA play?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA had a very crucial role -- a very crucial role in that period. They played a very crucial role because they were particularly interested in the Bosnian area for different reasons. First, because Bosnia backed -- they proclaimed Serb autonomous and then republic of Krajina, which was part of Croatia, but its border was a large part of Bosnia -- just if I can show you again?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're looking at exhibit number --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, coming back to exhibit 107 just to give -- this is the map. This was the area of the Serb Krajina while Sandzak was here, just to give you the reference point on the map. This was the reason why the JNA was interested in this area. When, for instance, in January, February 1992, the process of independence of Croatia was over and Croatia was recognised by the European Commission, and the cease-fire was complied with. The army had to withdraw from Croatia and they withdrew into Bosnia but knowing that they were back in an area which was not under the immediate control of Croatia. This was the Krajina area of Croatia. Secondly, in Bosnia, there were a lot of military industries from the time -- from Tito's time. They were a lot of military facilities. For this reason, it was important, Bosnia, for JNA. In addition, JNA started later to support, particularly, Serb regulars. This happened particularly in January, February 1992 when they started to distribute weapons, when they started ammunition and when they were backed by this document I mentioned before, this secret order coming from Blagoje Adzic, the acting Minister of Defence of the federal -- federation, the federation where the army had to put under its own command all the regulars in Bosnia. But I mentioned also in September 1991, the JNA called for mobilisation in Bosanska Krajina, the yellow area in the map, and this area was predominantly inhabited by Serbs. This created great concern and tensions between JNA and Izetbegovic and Izetbegovic and the government. After this mobilisation, which was followed by tanks and air explosions, incidents provoked by the Serbs in the area around Banja Luka, it follows in October the decision to declare the sovereignty of Bosnia. To make things worse, Izetbegovic didn't have inside connections, relations with the JNA. Communications with the command of JNA and Izetbegovic were very difficult. They didn't have connections. In this sense, they judged the position of the others, not having specific possibility of context to know what was going on. When the army, for instance, considered the action of Izetbegovic and the Parliament in Bosnia to declare the sovereignty of Bosnia, they reacted negatively and they started to organise, more or less, in the areas -- in various areas, just to keep the control around villages or around the towns. In addition, the JNA had several changes in that period. We are at the beginning of 1992. In 1992, January, in the beginning of January, a helicopter of the European Union was shot down near Cakovec, close to Cakovec, by Serb aircraft. This was the opportunity used by the Yugoslav leadership to compel Kadijevic to resign. Kadijevic was forced to resign and Blagoje Adzic became the acting Minister of Defence for the Yugoslav Federation. It was still existing while in December Markovic resigned. The federal government didn't exist yet. Blagoje Adzic was removed because he was known for his commitments in 1991 against Serb and Croat claims of cessation. This explained why Blagoje Adzic immediately in February sent this famous order, the order to the army in Bosnia, in order to keep the control immediately of the regular Serbs that had to act with the help of the JNA and receiving, of course, the military support of the JNA. Then, in May 1992, 38 Generals were forced to resign in Serbia. This was a very great change. This change also was followed by great pressure from the international community to withdraw Serb soldiers and arms from Bosnia. We are in May 1992. This means that the war already officially erupts all around Bosnia. According to Serb democratic sources, only 20 percent were aware of these arms and, generally, this was a cosmetic change. But because they started to say, okay, all people living in Bosnia and bordering Bosnia is a Bosnian citizen, so we can't oblige them not to fight for the Serb rights in Bosnia. This was the justification of the Serb government. However, they withdrew one part of the army. They changed 38 Generals in this period. This means that even on that occasion, even until May, there was resistance and difficulties in the Yugoslav Army, particularly in the high command, to completely adhere to the Serb policy of cessation from Yugoslavia. In demonstration, there is a very interesting document we have. In March, April, before the war in Croatia, a document from the General Milutin Kukanjac who was in charge in Bosnia, and he sent a document, a report, how the situation was in Bosnia during that period. He claimed and made clear that the Serbs were threatened and the army was ready to protect the Serbs from threats coming from the Croats and the Muslims, but he added, and this is very interesting, he added that, however, there are many attempts from the SDS leaders, so the Serb Democratic Party, the party of Karadzic, and from there it was entered into the local municipalities to have direct contacts with the Serb government in order to receive supplies, arms, health supplies and so on. This has to be stopped because the only relation can be through the federal government, not this direct relation of the local municipalities with a republic which is only part of the federation. In the mentality of this soldier, it's clear that he was thinking, again, of Yugoslavia, and he was writing to the federal Minister of Defence, not to the government -- and he asked the federal Minister of Defence to intervene with the government -- and speak to the government of Serbia in order to ask them to stop immediately this kind of direct connections between the government of Serbia and the local municipalities, which means that this was an odd mentality. These were people that were set aside after May 1992. This was a demonstration that's still in that period. There was a link, a communist link, with the idea of the federation. The idea of the federation in the army was different than the goals of the partition of Yugoslavia which was on the basis -- a real basis of the Yugoslav and Milosevic's goals, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have spoken of the JNA. What was the role played by the Territorial Defence in 1992 in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence in 1992, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, didn't play any significant role, didn't play any significant role because on the basis of the orders, you remember, the orders of the presidency, 23rd May, 1990, when Borisav Jovic was the president of the presidency of Yugoslavia, in Bosnia, the weapons protected in the stores in Bosnia on the chance of war was moved to the stores of the JNA and moved to the stores of the JNA with the approval of Izetbegovic. In this sense, the Territorial Defence was largely dismantled in Bosnia. They didn't have significant arms, weapons, ammunition, only just the remnants joined the army -- the remnants of the Territorial Defence joined the Bosnian army and created the Bosnian army in April, May 1992 when the war erupted and they must have had to create it and the Bosnians had to create an army. But this position of Izetbegovic was, in a sense, suggested by Izetbegovic because Izetbegovic at that time, 1990 and 1991 -- 1991, he supported the idea that Bosnia could remain in a Yugoslav Federation, whether both Croatia and Serbia will remain in this federation. This was his position. He changed often his opinions on this topic. This is one aspect in that period. This was one of the reasons why he didn't want to face -- to confront, to face immediately the army, the JNA, and accepted this dismantlement of the Territorial Defence. In addition, while the HDZ opposed strongly, the JNA was an occupational army. In this sense, they had two different positions. And what is interesting is that later, Izetbegovic was charged, I think -- I'm thinking even after the date when agreements were signed -- was charged for taking this decision, because he was accused of having dismantled Bosnia and of having offered Bosnia as a victim to the aggression of the Serbs without any weapons and without any arms. But the charge is based on the evaluation what happened afterwards. As a policy maker, evidently Izetbegovic tried to change or to make some difference at that moment and try to reduce the possibility of importing the war into Bosnia. So this is a very disputed evaluation that we can have in order to consider the decision of Izetbegovic in 1991 to accept this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the military and political involvement, if any, of Belgrade or the Republic of Serbia in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the course of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The involvement was, as I can say, double-face, from one side in the military -- from the military point of view and from the political point of view. From the military point of view, Serbia offered the real basis for the army, the army involved in the war in Bosnia. When the famous 20 percent of the 3 army was withdrawn from Bosnia, the other army remained, and this was why the reason was cosmetic, 5 as the army remained, not any more the JNA in Bosnia but the army of the Serb people in Bosnia fighting for their rights. And so Serbia offered real basis of -- sent drivers, sent weapons, fresh soldiers, ammunitions. We have a lot of documents. Even documents were published in Sarajevo showing that people fighting in Bosnia received their own wages and wages from the Serb government. So this -- clear military support offered from Serbia and Montenegro to the army, the Serb army, involved in the war in Bosnia. From the political point of view, this is a very important topic because this was connected to the idea of the meeting, the meeting -- or the idea of partition of Bosnia with Croatia. Before the war started in March 1991 in Karadjordjevo -- the Croat Tudjman and Milosevic met. We don't have, of course, the note verbal of the meeting.
