But after this meeting, when they made a decision to divide Bosnia in two parts, one for Croatia and the other one for Serbia, two Commissions were appointed by the two Presidents to meet and to discuss with the maps how to divide Bosnia. One of the person appointed to this Commission -- the members of the Serb Commission didn't give any information or any public report on this, while from the Croatian side, yes. This was Professor Dusan Bilandzic, a well professor and very old friend, personal friend, of Tudjman. I met him. I know him quite well, I met him in 1992, and he explained to me what happened during these meetings. But anyway, he gave an interview to the weekly -- Croat weekly "Nacional" last year, and he explained openly what happened. They met several times. They had opportunity to compare maps. They were unable to find a partition of Bosnia. So they tried to discuss how to divide Bosnia, but it was very difficult to establish the exact borders for -- under the interest of the -- of Croatia and Serbia. So this was the reason they tried to establish this agreement. They didn't succeed in finding a compromise But attempts to come to this agreement continued during the Bosnian wars. For instance, in May 1992, Boban and Karadzic met in Graz and tried -- this was May 1992, when the war in Bosnia had already erupted, and they discussed a possible agreement between the two. They met again in Njivice, which is an area close to Herceg-Novi in Montenegro, to find an agreement in 1993. So this was an attempt to come to an agreement between the two parties to divide Bosnia. In this sense, Serbia backed, of course, -- politically -- Karadzic and the military actions in Bosnia with the aim, evidently, of dividing Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, Professor, you have some maps there, not the next two, which point to the potential division of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There are -- we can take -- I wanted to explain to you in this sense the potential division because -- okay. If you want, we can take into consideration the maps included in the exhibit number 116 H, B, C, D.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A, B, C, D.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A, B, C, D. Yes. 116A -- I will show you. Ethnic division. This was an attempt of --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell us, on the back of each one, it indicates --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 116A, fine. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These maps can -- are interesting, particularly, when you compare the maps. So this was the ethnic division of Bosnia as it was agreed by SDA, HDZ, SDS. When they finally -- in the Konak. This is in Villa Konak; it happened immediately before the war erupted so -- and after the referendum, so February-March 1992, when the European Union, particularly under the direction of the Troika Cutiliero from Portugal, tried to establish the cantonisation of Bosnia, a cantonisation which was opposed by the leader of HDZ, Stjepan Kljujic. And for this reason, in February, he was compelled to resign from HDZ, and Mate Boban, who had at that moment the confidence of Tudjman, took over the direction of the party. And they tried to make this division of Bosnia, which didn't work particularly because the Democrats and part of the SDA were against any ethnic partition inside Bosnia, so they didn't oppose. But what is interesting is also, if you make a comparison of the three following maps, B, C, D, where you have first (indiscernible) Muslim-Croat concept, when you see that the Croat area is particularly related with Herzegovina and Posavina, these two areas, and the Muslim part is the Central Eastern -- connected with the Central Eastern Bosnia and the area of Bihac, this is the area of Bihac, this is the north-western part of Bosnia. So you can see that to the Serbs, according to the Muslim-Croatian concept of the division of that period, the Serbs had only north-western Bosnia and just some parts in Herzegovina and in the eastern -- on the right bank of the Drina River, in this area. While the Serb Democratic option -- this is Exhibit C -- clashes eminently with the other one. I don't know if it is possible to show comparatively. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible? Okay. Very good. You see the proposal, the Serb proposal, the Serb canton was -- it included all the north-western part of Bosnia plus a large part of the eastern part of Bosnia, which was -- in the Muslim Croatian idea was predominantly Croatian and Muslim. For Croatia you see only one part of Herzegovina close to Dalmatia, plus some islands in Central Bosnia and in Posavina. But you have also, and this is the case of "D" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "D" map. In the event that it was not possible to find an agreement with the Muslims, the Croats had their own map, and this map included, as you can see, it's not exactly the same area agreed between the Muslims and the Croats in the first -- in Exhibit B. If you make a comparison between Exhibit B and Exhibit D. You see that they claim toward the Central Bosnia is much more clear in the Croatian option than in the Croatian Muslim proposal. So if you compare these maps, prepared at the last moment when already the referendum was made, Bosnia was awaiting recognition from the European Union, the Serbs who are preparing to go to war, because Karadzic clearly stated, clearly stated that -- immediately after the referendum that Bosnia was facing a war. By the way, I can say that I met him personally in -- before the election in 1990 in the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo, and I had personally the impression that he already wanted a war at the time. So before the election, he was ready to provoke a war in Bosnia, and he was preparing himself for a war. I'm not personally -- personally, I'm not surprised at this declaration by Karadzic immediately after the referendum. But if you compare all these maps, you see how difficult it was. Even in the case of a partition -- this was not a partition, this was just to create ethnic cantons in Bosnia. It was not clear if the Serbs accepted independence of Bosnia or not, but anyway -- or to prepare the ethnic cantons in order to divide Bosnia later. This is different. But you can see from these maps how difficult the job was. I can imagine Dusan Bilandzic or the others discussing after March 1991, in June-July, so when the war erupted, a partition with Bosnia, when Bosnia was not in a war, just how difficult it was for them to divide the area. Taking into consideration that the sources of legitimisation for the claims were different, because they were based on demographic reasons, on historical reasons, on geo-political interests, communications and so forth. So different reasons interacted together in order to make these maps, and they clashed with each other as sources of legitimisation. So this was the real difficulty for policy makers and advisors of policy makers to find an agreement, an agreement amongst them, in order to find an ethnic solution, ethnic partition of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What then was the position taken, if any, by the international community to this conflict in 1992 in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally, the international community, in my opinion, had a very weak reaction. It was, in my opinion, unable to understand the dimension of the general disintegration of Yugoslavia. They were unable to understand what went on before the Yugoslav crisis and during the Yugoslav crisis, so before the war erupted in June 1991 and later on. There are many reasons why they were so weak and why they offered a weak solution for a long time. The first reason is a cultural one, in my opinion. They were unable to face a strong, national, even if national ethnic legitimisation of powers for the new secession State of Yugoslavia for policy makers, and probably we can't ask policy makers to have a clear distinction of biological and voluntary -- natural and voluntary idea of nations as I spoke when -- last time. So maybe -- the question is nation. Nation is a concept, very unclear concept. The claim for nationality, independent full nationality, prevented, in a sense, policy makers to understand immediately the real dimension of the war and of the claims to divide all Yugoslavia. This was one of the things. But the other thing is that the international community as a whole was very weakened because it was -- it had no common position. As, for instance, Germany and France, at the beginning, supported respectively Croatia and Serbia, albeit it's true that their support to these two countries diminished in the months to come. Italy. Italy was weakened dramatically because its own internal crisis of legitimation [sic]. It was the period when the corruption crisis started and 11 a ruling class was completely set aside in that period. Great Britain. Great Britain had a very weak position because many aspects of the questions connected to the Yugoslav framework had links with the situation in Ulster, and so the question had elements in this sense and they were not so interested to discuss this topic. So this is -- inside the states, the member states of the European Community which is, as is well-known, a community without a defence, a common defence and foreign policy. So they had to agree all together to find a common position in order to have then -- to have then a relation with the others. So considering this division within these countries, it's very difficult for them to find a compromise rapidly as the situation required. United States. The United States had made a decision -- decided for a long time to consider the Yugoslav question as a European issue. It didn't want to be involved in this question. It charged Europe to find a solution for this, but Europe wasn't able for the reasons I mentioned. The Islamic community. The Islamic community, albeit speaking about the Muslims threatened in Bosnia, they generally spoke about this, but they were very aware that any move they made in order to protect the Muslim community in Bosnia would be considered a confirmation of a showdown between Christianity and Islamic fundamentalism, as it was the propaganda of the Serb nationalism. So considering -- in addition, you have to consider that Saudi Arabia and Turkey had a different position than Iran, and so they controlled each other and division were very strong within the Islamic community too. So in this context, we have to take into consideration why the international community reacted so weakly and so poorly when the war erupted. Otherwise, when Communism collapsed, policy makers particularly in Europe were so happy, let me say, to have won the Cold War. They didn't understand immediately that with the collapse of Communism, a new question was arising. This question was the question of the legitimisation of powers in the new successor states or in the states -- former Communist states. This was very difficult for them to understand culturally. This is not because I wanted to make a clear justification. I just wanted to make clear why it is understandable, their weakness, and it is not a moral evaluation. This is not the question. This is just to understand the reason. So in this context, the United Nations, in the end, in September 1991, made a decision to impose an arms embargo on the whole of Yugoslavia which was, in fact -- which had, in fact, a negative impact particularly on the Muslim community because they were surrounded. They didn't have possibility to contact the external world through sea or boat, while it was easier even for the Croat and the Bosnian communities to receive weapons and army from Croatia and Serbia and through the borders anyway illegally to receive weapons and ammunition from outside. This was in September 1991. This was one of the reasons why this was often under discussion. The United States, particularly during the Clinton Presidency, tried to -- and asked to leave the embargo, the arms embargo. This was one of the discussions in the United States for a long time. Then the United Nations in 1992 -- this was in 1991. In 1992, the United Nations first, in the beginning of April, for the first time, deployed peace keepers in Krajina. This was the first military intervention of the international community in the conflict when the UN peace keepers had to be deployed in the areas between Croatia and Krajina and in Krajina. And then, as it was established later in May 1992, the end of May, with Resolution 757, sanctions were established against Serbia and Montenegro. These sanctions were later strengthened. This was an attempt to isolate Serbia and Montenegro completely as they were recognised as being most responsible for the war. Immediately after -- this was at the end of May. In June, Resolution 758 established a -- the action -- the participation of UN peace keepers in the airport of Sarajevo as an airport, an international airport; and later in October, another resolution established a no-fly zone over Bosnia, over the skies of Bosnia. So in this sense, because they -- and then the UNPROFOR representatives had opportunity to send reports to the United Nations when illegal flights from Serbia and Croatia often were noticed by time -- particularly during the night. So this was the first reaction of the international community in that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the 26th of August, 1992, were the participants in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina summonsed to a peace conference in London?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was a conference in -- it was the consequence of the conference -- the continuation of the conference chaired by Lord Carrington in The Hague in 1991 and it was continued in London in 1992, and then, because no agreement was found in London, this conference moved to Geneva in September 1992. There were attempts at calling all the parties, Milosevic, Tudjman, and representatives of the Bosnian leaderships, to find a solution, but the solution was not found at that time. These were the international conferences organised with this in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were new mediators appointed as a consequence of this conference held in August and September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In which --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were Robert Owen and Cyrus Vance appointed as mediators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, okay, because they were charged to prepare a proposal for a solution to Bosnia, and they prepared a plan that was submitted to the members -- to the parties, the conflicting parties at the beginning of January, 1993, the 2nd of January, the proposal for partition -- for the reorganisation of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we want to move to the area directly involved in this particular case, the conflict between the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, and can you tell us when tensions first occurred between these two groups, the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims and how it developed, and I think you have to go back some time in order to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we have to go back again, sorry, chronologically. Yeah. Officially, openly, tensions started to arise in autumn 1991 when -- in October, after the 15th of October, the declaration of sovereignty was voted by HDZ and SDS leaderships. A few days after, the President of HDZ, Stjepan Kljujic, gave an interview to the Croatian newspaper from Rijeka, "Nova List," and this interview was particularly interesting because it envisaged a change of strategy for the HDZ. We have to consider the period. We are in October 1991. This is the fall 1991. This is the period when Dubrovnik was bombarded and Vukovar was besieged and then the Serb army entered Vukovar. So in this context, Stjepan Kljujic started to explain that probably it should be better for the Muslims and the Croats to distinguish their fate from that of the Serbs even in Bosnia. A few days earlier, I mentioned the declaration of sovereignty was voted only by Croats and Muslims. So he suggested this, and he suggested that this distinction of the fate had to be considered in the framework of a possible future confederation with Slovenia and Croatia, with Slovenia, or otherwise creating an independent separate state. Speculation and discussion immediately followed in Bosnia about this position of Kljujic, and some weeks later, at the beginning of November, it was maybe much more clear why Kljujic started to speak to this when the first Croatian autonomous region was created. So in this moment, when this declaration of Kljujic in "Novi List" was reported by the newspapers and by public opinion in Bosnia, tensions between Croats and Muslims arose, and this was the first official tension that emerged between the two communities in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you have a map there, do you not, exhibit 110?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have a map of the Croat -- this is the map, exhibit 110. This is the map of the process of creating -- of creating the areas of the Croat community, autonomous communities, the so-called -- Croat community, Hrvatska Zajednica. Because the process was similar to that of the Serb autonomous region, the so-called SAO. Later in the political terminology, this was called the HAO process, so the SAO and the HAO. HAO is the Croat, Haoizacija. So Haoizacija and Saoizacija were the two terms used by political scientists to speak about this process of reorganisation of ethnic communities in Bosnia. The first community that was established was Bosanska Posavina, the yellow one in the north close to the Sava River. This was established on -- 12th, November 12th, 1991, and reactions were -- the concerns particularly between Muslim community and those of the Bosnian who share the idea of a -- Bosnians of citizens and the whole Bosnia to be defended, their concerns dramatically increased. What is interesting was the reaction of a part of the HDZ leadership. The head of HDZ Mostar reacted -- explained that, "Okay, this is just an attempt of organising the Serbs locally for economic and cultural reasons, but it doesn't mean anything because the majority of the population emotionally related -- connected to the idea of Croatia, and Croatia is in Herzegovina -- it's around this area. And there are no proclamation of Herzegovinian Croat community at all, so this was just in that area, and the demonstration -- they wanted to show that this was not the process. Unfortunately, two days after this declaration, the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna was proclaimed, and it was created, you will see, in this red area. This is the red area. This is an area with a long border with Croatia. This is Dalmatia in this area and the Dubrovnik area, while this -- also Slavonia for the Posavina. So both regions had borders with Croatia, albeit Posavina was separated by a river and there was no division, geographical division, between Herceg-Bosna and Croatia. And then, late in January, another Croat community, the Croat community of Srednja Bosnia, was created. This is the blue one. So three Croatian communities were established between November and January while the Serb communities were established between September and January 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think the next map, exhibit 111, what does that relate to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was a map -- I wanted -- I prepared myself. This one. It was -- this area is a comparison between the two previous maps, exhibit 110 and 107, between the two -- the two claimed -- between the two maps with the areas claimed by the Croat community and the Serb autonomous community. Just to give you an idea of the areas claimed by both the two communities, the two, the Serb and the Croat communities, all not claimed by both, the two communities. So the green areas in this map, the green areas, are the areas not claimed either by Bosnian Serbs or Bosnian Croats, and you see it is just one area in the Bihac area which was surrounded by the Serbs because this route here was the -- Drina River, this was the area claimed by the Croats -- by the Serbs, sorry, and just some islands around Sarajevo, Srebrenica, Virovitica, and Tuzla, just these areas. While the red one were the areas included both in the Serb autonomous region and in the Croat community. This can explain, for instance, the reaction of Karadzic when HDZ started to create these communities. He supported the idea. He was not against the idea of creating Croat community in Bosnia. He was against the pretension [sic] of the Croat community on some areas, Kladanj, on the other side, by Karadzic himself. So this was the question. This was about the two -- so this can also offer a picture to you in order to understand why it was so difficult to establish a partition, a division, of the maps of Bosnia, because even in a context -- even in a peaceful context, at least for Bosnia, the two maps claimed by Croat community and Serb community clash with each other at least in one, two, three, four, five areas, which means more districts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any historical foundation to these respective claims by both Serbia -- by both the Bosnian Serbs and perhaps even Serbia and the Bosnian Croats and perhaps Croatia, and do you have any maps there that touch upon this historical claim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. As I told you previously, when the question of the creation of the new state was on the table, the issue of legitimisation of powers became a crucial issue, and it was based on different clashing claims, historical, demographic, economic reasons, claims, legitimisation. History played a very important role because history is considered on the basis of the natural idea of nation, on the basis of -- the biological idea of nations. It is based on the state or ancient state created in the Middle Ages and then destroyed by the great empires or on the basis of some kind of recognition, international recognition, received in the past. So, for instance, I have here different maps that I can show you in this sense. These are the exhibit number 112, 113, 114, 115; that can be also considered in a comparative way just to understand the different idea. You know, when Mate Boban spoke about -- immediately after the creation of the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna, he wanted to stress in his public reports, meetings, he wanted to stress the right of the Croat people to live in the historical and to create -- the historical borders, to implement the historical dreams of the Croats to live in a state, in a Croat State. So when you speak about history, historical, you know something because immediately -- although it can be strange for us -- immediately you create a condition from the other side, the Muslim, the Serbs, to react in the same way. So history is a very -- or the manipulation or the interpretation of history is often a political tool in order to establish a legitimisation on some area. So, for instance, exhibit 112 can offer one of the areas claimed by Boban when he supported and he explained the reason why the Herceg-Bosna community, Croat community, was created. He mentioned in his speeches the so-called Banovina, Croat Banovina, of 1939. This is the area you can see -- it is the red-line area -- this was the Banovina of Croatia. This Banovina of Croatia was created after an agreement, an agreement in 1939 between the Serb and the Croat representatives of the so-called agreements, Sporazum Cvetkovic-Macek, the two persons who agreed to create this map. They decided -- this was in 1939, please, just on the eve of the beginning of the Second World War when Hitler was already threatening Poland, so it was in August-September -- July-August, something, and this area was created as an autonomous banate. "Banate" means the area of a province, from the term "Ban" who was the governor of Croatia in the ancient past. So this Banovina was an autonomous province created from some of the previous Banovina. When King Alexander carried his coup in 1929, the first thing was to create administrative reform of the country, and he wanted to destroy the different -- Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia and create Banovina on the main tributaries of the rivers, so you can see here Banate of Drava, Banate of Vrbas -- these are rivers -- Banate of Drina. So Banate of Sava was the River Sava and Banate of Primorje -- "Primorje" means the coast, the shores. And so this was the reason why he made this. And then King Alexander was killed by a terrorist Ustashe in 1939, and later, in -- sorry, 1934. And in 1939, an agreement was reached by the Serb and Croatian representatives to create an autonomous Banate of Croatia including Sava and Primorje, plus some area of Bosnia, you can see, on the south of Sava and on the north of Primorje, these two areas. So this was the -- one -- in this sense, as you can see, particularly this part, is not so far from the autonomous region of Herceg-Bosna if you make a comparison with the exhibit 110 just -- you can make a comparison and you can see this sense and you can see this part and this part. So when Boban spoke about Banovina, he had a clear idea in his mind and it was very well understood by people, by Croats and by the others, of course. Otherwise, if this was a claim by Boban in that period, the claim of the Chetniks, particularly Serbia, Serbs, Chetniks, you can see in this map was more or less similar to these --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's exhibit --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, that exhibit is 113. Just to -- this is an historical map. It's not just a map of the claims of Seselj. Seselj was, and still is, the President of the Radical Party of Serbia, the party which claims historical links with the Chetnik movement. The Chetniks were, in fact, the soldiers of the King of Serbia, so they were Serb nationalists. And, in fact, immediately after the first dismemberment of Yugoslavia in 1941, when the Nazi army enter Yugoslavia, the Chetniks or, better, the soldiers and the officials loyal to the King who was in exile in London, organised themselves in Chetnik groups, and they joined the area between Serbia and Bosnia, and one of them, a lawyer, the lawyer, Stefan Moljevic, prepared a map for the future re-establishment of Yugoslavia, moreover a (indiscernible) of the Chetniks, and you can see in this map the idea of Yugoslavia, of the Chetniks of Draza Mihajlovic and the Chetniks fighting during the Second World War, which was re-used by the Chetniks and by Seselj after, in 1991, 1992. So they wanted to -- they claimed a possible Yugoslavia for the end of the Second World War with a Great Serbia, which included, as you can see, Macedonia, increasingly and interestingly enough a part of Albania, you can see, (in foreign language) -- I don't know in English "Scutari." This is the area denoted by Albania and Dalmatia, you can see, and even a part of Slovenia, while Croatia was the great victim of this map. As you can see, Croatia was divided in two areas only, two areas not territorially connected, this one part in Slovenia, one part in Croatia proper, and he was punished, even losing control of the Rijeka port which was offered to Slovenia, and this reason was because, from the Chetnik point of view, Croatia supported during the war the enemy, German Nazis, so Croatia had to be punished for this reason, and for this reason, Croatia was restricted to this part. So this map offered an idea of what was the claim, the historical claims, of the Chetniks when the war was yet to be started, and the idea was to leave Croatia and Slovenia abandoned and to flee the country. But, in comparison -- Croatia, Serbia had been established on this area, including also Dalmatia and this was the famous line from Virovitica, Karlobag and Karlovac that had to divide Croatia from Serbia, from Serbia. This was the war goal of the Chetniks. But, you see, often Chetniks and the Serbs claimed that, just to give you an idea, this was one claim. But otherwise they insisted that everywhere where there is a Serb monument is, is Serbia. And for instance -- this is a joke, but interesting enough, Ratko Mladic, during the war, claimed that Trieste is a Serb town because -- and, in fact, it's true -- there is a Serb Orthodox Church in Trieste. But, as you know, in Trieste you have also a synagogue and Greek Orthodox Church and other churches, so it's very difficult in a sense if everybody pretended to run on the business of the monuments. But, anyway, it can be a joke for us, but it was serious for them and it was dramatically serious in this sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Professor, we only have five minutes less --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last two maps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last two maps, if we could quickly just dispose of those, I think --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to show a map of Croatia in -- this is the -- exhibit number 114, how Croatia was in -- when Croatia joined the Yugoslav State in 1918 on -- this was the Croatia in 1918, but you have to take into account that Croatia was unified under Yugoslavia. This is very important to stress this. Croatia was unified because Dalmatia was part of the Austrian Empire while the other part of Croatia was under the Hungarian part of the Empire, and after the agreement, the agreement between -- after 1867, only the dynastic union was the element of unification for the Austro-Hungarian Empire. So the unification of Croatia was possible within Yugoslavia, and you can see even that one part of Banja is not in Croatia, it was a part of Hungary, now Banja is in Croatia, while Croatia controlled completely the area of Srjem just to Belgrade, because this was the frontier -- the border between the Austro-Hungarian Empire and the Ottoman Empire and Serbia, later on. So sometimes when you find also the claims of Croatia to join -- to have its own rights, to have the borders on the Danube River, it does mean that only Danube is Banja, is Banja or the area, this area that is Vukovar or Osijek, but can be interpreted also, if not clarified, to control all Srjem until Belgrade, which is one of the reasons of possible clashes between the two, Croatia and Serbia, when they speak about history.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And finally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- exhibit 115.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This was the last exhibition map, this 115, and this was the Croatian independent state established by Nazis and Fascist powers during the Second World War. You can see on this map, what is very interesting is that Dalmatia, large part of Dalmatia, was not included in Croatia because it was claimed by Italy, and this is one of the reasons why the Ustashe, which was supported by Mussolini before the war, became much more -- leaned and aligned with the Germans because they were disappointed with this claim of Italy, while they included completely all Bosnia, as you can see, and the border is Drina, so Drina has been claimed often as the correct and regular border between Serbs and Croats. This is Drina. It's interestingly enough to have also two terms when you speak about the Serbs. The Serbs on the left bank of Drina and the Serbs on the right bank of Drina have two different names. They are called "Serbi" when you speak about the Serbs in Bosnia -- or in Croatia, and "Serbianci" when you speak about the Serbs in Serbia. And so this -- interesting enough. And this is the Drina River, and this includes also, as you can see, Srbija completely, just join the area close to Belgrade. This is until -- this is the suburb of Belgrade. You can -- new Belgrade would be part of this area where it is today, new Belgrade. So it is just to give you an idea how complicated it is when you speak about the historical dream on -- the historical borders of Croatia. This is something quite -- that create immediately concern on the others as well as you have the same reaction when the Serbs claim their own -- Great Serbia and the dream of the Serbs to live in the same state, you know? This is -- when you manipulate the maps in the past in order to legitimise a political claim of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we have finished for today, and tomorrow we will resume in the second courtroom. Good afternoon to all of you.
